newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: SPROUT FARMER SPRINTS TO GLORY IN GREAT SKATE RACE.
newsitem.headline: SPROUT FARMER SPRINTS TO GLORY IN GREAT SKATE RACE.

text.p: A 29-year-old sprout farmer became a Dutch national hero on Saturday by turning on a powerful final sprint to win a gruelling 200 km (125 mile) skating marathon.

Henk Angenent completed the rarely held race across the frozen canals of the northern Netherlands in just under seven hours and less than two metres (six feet) ahead of his nearest rival, crane driver and pre-race favourite Erik Hulzebosch.
"This is the best day of my life," he said after leading the field of more than 16,000 skaters home.
The Eleven Cities marathon can only be held during severe winters when ice thickness reaches at least 15 cms (six inches) along the entire course which links 11 mediaeval Friesian towns.
First held in 1909, this year's race was only the 15th this century and the first after a gap of 11 years.
In Friesland province half a million fans turned out to watch the race which is regarded as both a major sporting occasion and a national festival.

Many of them partied deep into the night on Friday in the provincial capital of Leeuwarden, where the race traditionally starts and finishes, and the revelry was expected to continue well into the early hours of Sunday morning.

Throngs of people in orange bobble-hats lined the route, keeping warm to the steady beat of local oompah bands and shouting encouragement to the competitors. Millions more watched live television coverage from the comfort of their own homes.
The race began well before dawn with the first group of 300 top marathon skaters being released from a steel cage and emerging into the darkness and freezing cold.
Over the next few hours thousands of "tourist class" skaters set off at regular intervals, hoping only to complete the race and recount their personal tales of heroism and endurance.

Over a third of the field were aged over 50, including 1954 race winner Jeen van den Berg, 69, who was competing for the seventh time. The oldest skater was born in 1918 as the First World War drew to a close while the youngest had just turned 18.
The last contestants were due to reach the finishing line around midnight, but many were expected to give up before then.
Angenent is assured of hero status but his material rewards are likely to be modest compared with other top sporting stars.
Evert van Benthem, winner of the previous two races in 1985 and 1986, continues to work as a dairy farmer even though his double victory catapulted him to fame.
But the workaday lifestyles of the Eleven Cities champions are all part of the charm, harking back to a more innocent age when sportsmen competed for honour rather than financial gain.
Despite the absence of major commercial sponsorship deals, the race was a smoothly run event, staged by an army of volunteers within 48 hours of its announcement on Thursday.
